single_story.note: One story: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute rated OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens an 'Unacceptable Risk' on Oct 7, 2026, and OpenAI disputed the testing.

the_news.text: On Oct. 7, 2026, Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute rated OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens an 'Unacceptable Risk' and urged OpenAI to restrict ChatGPT to adults 18+ until fixed. OpenAI disputes the testing.

why_it_matters.text: Parents may believe built-in teen alerts and limits protect their kids when, per the assessment, the alerts did not fire in tests on crisis conversations (an assessment OpenAI disputes).
The dispute is over methodology and timing of parental-control activation. That affects whether the central finding (no alerts) holds up, and it shows why independent testing is being demanded.

facts.text: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens an 'Unacceptable Risk' on Oct. 7, 2026, saying OpenAI's new teen protections fall short of what the company promised.
notes: Common Sense Media is the assessor, not a neutral wire; its findings are its own testing.

facts.text: The Institute says OpenAI should restrict ChatGPT to users 18 and older until it fixes the gaps, and that the fixes should be independently tested by third parties.

[CLAIM: Common Sense Media says] Testers spent up to an hour discussing suicidal ideation, self-harm or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts, and the linked parent accounts got zero alerts; notifications could only be prompted on much older accounts with weeks of sensitive-topic history.
notes: Gizmodo quotes the report: none of the test accounts produced a notification within the one-hour window OpenAI has identified as its target.
OpenAI disputes the testing method (see F9).

facts.text: [CLAIM: Common Sense Media says] ChatGPT failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis contact a hotline or professional, missed more than one in four warranted crisis referrals, and fell below the Institute's 95% threshold on three of five severe harms it treats as 'Red Lines'.
notes: Futurism notes experts rated the substance of mental-health responses as often good and 'clinically sound' but crisis responses uneven.

facts.text: [CLAIM: Common Sense Media says] Study Mode often showed a 'Show me the answer' pop-up that completed homework, and teens could leave parent-set Study Hours by deleting the @study prefix.

[CLAIM: Common Sense Media says] Despite a new Under-18 model spec, ChatGPT for Teens still expressed feelings, preferences and moods and interacted in relational ways, implying 'reciprocity' and 'mutuality'.
notes: 'Reciprocity'/'mutuality' wording is from Robbie Torney via Futurism.

facts.text: [CLAIM: Common Sense Media says] Age estimation did not work: adult-registered test accounts never switched to the teen experience, even when testers said they were 13 and the bot acknowledged this.
Some protections worked: the report found ChatGPT for Teens was successful at curbing romantic and sexual roleplay.
notes: Gizmodo says it was less firm on other boundaries such as health advice and violent roleplay.

facts.text: OpenAI pushed back, saying through spokesperson Eric Porterfield that the bulk of Common Sense's testing 'may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete,' making findings inaccurate.
notes: OpenAI hedges ('may have'; 'If that was the case').

facts.text: Common Sense Media replied that it confirmed with OpenAI before testing that the teen features were fully launched; OpenAI disclosed after the tests that alerts can take several hours to activate on newly linked accounts. Common Sense says some accounts were linked longer than that and still got no notifications.
notes: Futurism attributes it to 'Common Sense Media'; The Verge attributes it to Tom Siegel.

facts.text: The Institute disclosed it is funded by philanthropy and industry, including the OpenAI Foundation and makers of some technologies it evaluates, and says it keeps full editorial independence.
notes: Self-disclosure; only in Common Sense's press release among opened sources.

facts.text: Futurism reports the two groups collaborated as recently as 2024, and that in January OpenAI backed a youth AI safety bill authored by Common Sense Media.
notes: Single source.

facts.text: Common Sense advises families to talk to kids about the risks and not to rely on built-in protections and alerts; it also recommends OpenAI embrace age verification, which Futurism notes privacy advocates say carries its own privacy risks.
notes: Age-verification recommendation is reported by Futurism.

background.text: OpenAI announced ChatGPT for Teens in August (Aug. 18 per Common Sense), applying automatically to users 13 to 17 with parental notifications, a Study Mode, quiet hours and other guardrails.
notes: The date Aug. 18 comes from Common Sense Media's press release.

background.text: OpenAI faced a wrongful-death lawsuit last year from a California couple who said ChatGPT assisted their 16-year-old son's suicide. OpenAI then said safeguards may 'degrade' in long conversations.
notes: Single source; allegation by the family.

quotes.text: ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work,
quotes.speaker: Tom Siegel
quotes.where: Common Sense Media press release / statement, Oct. 7, 2026
notes: Verge renders it as 'ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don’t work,'.

quotes.text: A teen can spend an hour talking about self-harm without their parent getting a single alert. Until OpenAI fixes that and proves it with independent testing, ChatGPT should be for adults only.
quotes.speaker: Tom Siegel
quotes.where: Common Sense Media press release, Oct. 7, 2026

quotes.text: You can talk to ChatGPT as a teenager for up to an hour about suicide, self-harm, or various varying types of eating disorders, and ChatGPT will tell you that it’s not going to tell anybody about your conversations, and you will get no parental notifications.
quotes.speaker: Robbie Torney
notes: ⚠ single source

quotes.text: It is incumbent for OpenAI to earn the trust of parents and to show them, not just tell them, that this product is safe for teens to use,
quotes.speaker: Robbie Torney
notes: ⚠ single source

quotes.text: Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate. If that was the case, the tests would not establish whether parental safety notifications work as designed.
quotes.speaker: OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield
notes: Verge attributes it to Porterfield; Futurism attributes it to OpenAI.

quotes.text: We stand behind our testing methodology and our results.
quotes.speaker: Tom Siegel
quotes.where: Response to OpenAI, shared with The Verge
notes: ⚠ single source. Futurism attributes a similar response ('We stand by our interpretation of the results') to Common Sense Media.

quotes.text: Prior to release, we shared our evaluation results with OpenAI in good faith to allow it to improve its product.
quotes.speaker: Tom Siegel
notes: Futurism attributes it to Common Sense Media.

numbers.counts: Prompts tested on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds, before and after the Aug. 18 launch
notes: Futurism cites 990 prompts pre-launch and 450 post-launch for the notification count, a different tally.

numbers.counts: Times reviewers triggered parental notifications: twice out of 990 prompts before launch, twice out of 450 after, only on older accounts
notes: Single source.

numbers.counts: Warranted crisis referrals missed across tested mental-health conditions
Severe-harm 'Red Lines' where ChatGPT fell below the Institute's 95% threshold
Age range of users placed in ChatGPT for Teens
Time OpenAI says its systems can take to activate parental notifications on newly linked accounts (per Common Sense)

terms.name: ChatGPT for Teens
terms.definition: OpenAI's teen experience for users 13 to 17, with parental notifications, Study Mode, quiet hours and an Under-18 behavior spec; Futurism describes it as a version of ChatGPT with 'stronger built-in protections'.

terms.name: Study Mode
terms.definition: A feature that uses guiding questions and step-by-step help instead of simply giving answers; parents can set 'study hours' when it is on by default.

terms.name: Unacceptable Risk
terms.definition: The Youth AI Safety Institute's worst rating tier for an AI product.

terms.name: Age estimation / prediction
terms.definition: OpenAI's approach of inferring from usage whether a user is under 18 and then giving them the teen experience; Futurism distinguishes it from age verification.
